What Is Diabetes?

High Blood Pressure and Diabetes · Lesson 4

What Is Diabetes?

A flipchart for Care Group meetings. Show the picture side to the group. Turn to the text side to read the story, the questions and the messages.

  • Next and Back, or a swipe, turn the page.
  • Tap a picture to make it fill the screen.
  • Text shows what the facilitator reads. Picture goes back.

Lesson 4 at a glance

90 minutes. Bring the attendance registers and this flipchart. The Activity Leader brings chalk or a stick, five small stones and five bottle tops.

SectionMinutes
1. Game: Groups Of5
2. Attendance and troubleshooting10
3 and 4. Story and questions Picture 4.110
5. Too Much Sugar Stays in the Blood Picture 4.210

Total90

Before the pictures

Game: Groups Of. Everyone walks around. Call out a number. People quickly form groups of that number. Call other numbers. Finish with one circle.

Recall Lesson 3. Blood pressure is the push of the blood on the blood vessels. You cannot feel it. It harms the brain, the eyes, the heart and the kidneys. Control protects the body.

Commitments. Ask: “What was your commitment at the last lesson? Have you been able to keep it?”

After the pictures

Body Map with Stones. Draw the outline of a person on the ground.

  • Ask: “Where does high sugar harm the body?” Participants put a stone on the eyes, the heart, the kidneys, a hand (for the nerves) and a foot.
  • Ask: “Where does high blood pressure harm the body?” Participants put a bottle top on the brain, the eyes, the heart and the kidneys.
  • Ask: “Which places have both?” The eyes, the heart and the kidneys. “A person who has both conditions has more to protect.”
  • Ask: “What takes the stones and the bottle tops away?” Each time someone names one of the Four Helpers and shows its sign, she removes two or three. Continue until the map is clear.

Discuss barriers. Ask: “Is there anything that might prevent you from asking for a sugar check, or from showing a sore on your foot to the health worker?”

Request commitments. Ask: “Based on what you have heard today, what commitment will you make?” Each person chooses. Do not press anyone who is not ready.

Picture 4.1Story: Uncle Kofi’s Sore

Picture 4.1 · text sideStory: Uncle Kofi’s Sore

Read the story aloud.

Uncle Kofi drives his trotro from morning to night. These days he is always thirsty. He drinks many sachets of water, and he stops often to pass urine. He is tired. He says, “It is the heat. It is the work.”

One evening, his grandson Kwame sees a sore on Kofi’s foot. Kwame says, “Grandpa, this sore has been here since last month.” Kofi hides his foot. “It is nothing.”

Auntie Naa has been listening. She remembers that Kofi takes his medicine only when he “feels the sugar”. She says, “Kofi, tomorrow we go to the mission hospital together. They will check my pressure and your sugar.”

Ask the group.

  • What signs did Uncle Kofi have? What did he think caused them?
  • What do people in our community say causes sugar disease?
  • What do people here do when they think their sugar is high?

Encourage discussion. Do not correct “wrong” answers. Let everyone give an opinion. This page is for discussion, not for teaching.

Say “Let us compare your ideas with the messages on the following pages.”

Picture 4.2Too Much Sugar Stays in the Blood

Picture 4.2 · text sideToo Much Sugar Stays in the Blood

Ask: “What do you think these pictures mean?” Affirm the answers. Then share each message.

A

Food gives the body sugar. The body uses sugar for strength.

  • Much of the food we eat becomes sugar in the blood: kenkey, banku, rice, yam, bread and sweet drinks.
  • The blood carries the sugar to every part of the body.
  • The body makes a helper called insulin. Insulin moves the sugar from the blood into the body, where it gives strength.
B

In diabetes, too much sugar stays in the blood.

  • The body does not make enough insulin, or the insulin does not work well.
  • The sugar stays in the blood, and the body does not get its strength.
  • Eating sugar is not the only cause. Diabetes can run in families. Too much body weight and too little movement raise the chance.
C

Signs of high sugar: great thirst, passing urine often, tiredness.

  • Other signs are losing weight without trying, sight that is not clear, and sores that heal slowly.
  • Many people have no signs for years. The only way to know is a blood test.

Ask the group.

  • Which of these signs have you or someone in your family had?
  • What do people here do when they have these signs?
Additional information for the facilitator

Kinds of diabetes. Most adults with diabetes have the kind called type 2, which this lesson describes. Some people, often children and young adults, have type 1: the body makes no insulin and they need insulin injections from the start. Some women have high sugar during pregnancy. Do not ask participants which kind they have.

No blame. Do not let the group blame a person for her diabetes. Many causes are outside a person’s control.

Signs. The World Health Organization lists these signs: feeling very thirsty, needing to urinate more often than usual, blurred vision, feeling tired and losing weight without trying. The signs of type 2 diabetes can be mild and may take several years to be noticed.

Ants. People may say that ants gather where a person with diabetes has passed urine. This can happen when sugar is high, but it is not a test. Only a blood test shows the sugar.

Picture 4.3High Sugar Slowly Harms the Body

Picture 4.3 · text sideHigh Sugar Slowly Harms the Body

Ask: “What do you think these pictures mean?” Affirm the answers. Then share each message.

A

Year after year, high sugar harms the eyes, the heart, the kidneys, the nerves and the feet.

  • High sugar damages the small blood vessels and the nerves.
  • The harm comes slowly and quietly, like the harm from high blood pressure.
B

Sores on the feet heal slowly. Show any sore to the health worker early.

  • The feet lose feeling, so a person does not notice a small cut or sore.
  • A sore that is not treated can grow deep. Some people lose a toe or a foot.
C

When you control your sugar, you protect your body.

  • The Four Helpers bring the sugar down and keep it down.
  • Many people with diabetes also have high blood pressure. Ask for both checks.

Ask the group.

  • Kofi said the sore was nothing. What can we tell him now?
  • Who looks at your feet?
Additional information for the facilitator

Sources. The World Health Organization states that diabetes causes blindness, kidney failure, heart attacks, stroke and lower limb amputation.

Later lessons. Lesson 21 covers blood sugar that is too low or very high. Lesson 22 covers care of the feet. Lesson 23 covers the eyes, the kidneys and the heart.

Do not frighten. Some participants may know a person who has lost a foot. Let them speak, then return to the third picture: control protects the body.
